pages.title: Your Game Plan for Surgery
pages.description: Real surgical preparation starts before pre-op instructions arrive. See how concierge nursing support helps patients prepare for surgery and discharge home safely.

blocks.html:
Most families think of surgery as the day itself. You prepare for parking, the check-in desk, the waiting room, and meeting the surgeon. In our experience, your preparation for surgery begins well before that. This is the kind of preparation that rarely makes it onto any pre-op instruction sheet, but it shapes how the whole day, and following days, unfold.

The Weeks Before

Yes, weeks. True surgical preparation starts long before the pre-op instructions arrive. Adequate sleep and rest in the days leading up to a procedure support your body's ability to heal and respond well to the stress of surgery. Proper nutrition, steady hydration, and adequate protein intake in the weeks before a procedure give your body a stronger baseline for recovery. Preparation isn't only physical. Patients and families who set realistic expectations tend to move through the day with far less anxiety than those who don't. None of this is written on a pre-op checklist. This is why we created this post for your reference. This guide, in combination with your pre-op instructions, will leave you set up for success.

Final Preparations: NPO, Medications, & Vitals

As the procedure approaches, the instructions become a bit more specific. NPO or “nothing by mouth” means following specific instructions about when to stop eating and drinking before surgery. Fasting instructions may differ for solid food and clear liquids and depend on the procedure and your health. Follow the instructions from your surgical and anesthesia team, and ask them to clarify anything that is unclear. This pre-op order exists for a real physiological reason: an empty stomach reduces the risk of aspiration under anesthesia. Even a small lapse can mean a delayed or cancelled procedure.

Medications require their own careful attention. Certain medications need to be paused in the days beforehand. Others need to be taken exactly on schedule the morning of. Getting either direction wrong carries real risk, and the instructions aren't always clear to someone outside of healthcare.

  • “Wait, but wouldn’t taking my blood pressure medication on the morning of my procedure violate the doctor’s NPO order?”

    Answer: Your surgical or anesthesia team may instruct you to take certain medications with a small sip of water. Confirm which medicines to take, which to hold, and how to take them. Do not change your medication schedule or fasting instructions on your own.

  • If instructions are not clear on taking/not taking your scheduled medications, ALWAYS call the hospital or surgery center to clarify. The clinical team would much rather you call instead of risk having your case cancelled or delaying other cases that are on the schedule.

We also advise families to keep a simple daily log of blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation in the days prior to surgery. This isn't about diagnosing anything. It's about noticing. Out-of-range vitals can directly affect how anesthesia is administered, or whether a procedure can proceed as planned at all. A blood pressure reading that seems unremarkable to a family member three days out may be exactly the kind of detail a surgical team needs to hear.

The Morning Of

Arrival time is one of the least negotiable details in the entire process. Surgical schedules are built tightly around each other, and a single late arrival can ripple through an entire day of cases. Knowing exactly where to go, what to bring, and what to leave at home removes one more source of friction. For the family waiting nearby, simply understanding the shape of the day, how long the wait might be, and when they can expect to hear something, makes the waiting itself much easier to manage.

Why This All Matters

Here is the piece that ties everything together: a surgeon's decision to send a patient home after a procedure, rather than admit them overnight, is built on more than how the surgery itself went. It's built on confidence that someone reliable is standing behind the patient once they leave the building.

When a patient doesn't have dependable transportation or support waiting for them at home, many surgeons and proceduralists will choose to admit overnight rather than risk a discharge that isn't safe. It's a real clinical decision that is made every day, and it hinges on exactly the kind of preparation and support we’ve described above.

Everything in the weeks and hours before a procedure, the rest, the diet, the fasting, the medications, the vitals log, the punctual arrival, builds toward that moment. Dependable support at home isn't a courtesy extended to the patient. It's often part of what makes discharge home possible in the first place.

For additional guidance on preparing yourself or a loved one for surgery, Request Private Consultation.

pages.title: What Families Should Ask Before Hiring a Concierge Nurse
pages.description: Most families have never hired a concierge nurse and don't know where to start. These are the questions worth asking — and what to listen for in the answers.

blocks.html:
Concierge nursing is a relatively new category of care, and most families encounter it without a clear frame of reference for what to expect or how to evaluate it. This post is meant to provide families with a guided framework of questions to ask once a decision has been made to move forward with concierge nursing care. I invite you to explore my post Beyond Home Health: A Different Approach to Aging at Home to understand what concierge nursing is and how it differs from traditional home health and caregiving services.

What is your clinical background?

This is where every conversation should start. Concierge nursing is unregulated as a category, which means the credentials and experience behind the service vary widely. At minimum, you're looking for a licensed registered nurse. Beyond licensure, ask about the clinical setting they trained and worked in.

There's a meaningful difference between a nurse whose background is in acute hospital care and one whose experience is limited to lower-acuity settings. Neither is disqualifying, but the distinction matters when you're trusting someone to recognize a change in condition, interpret a medication interaction, or know when something warrants escalation.

Ask directly. A nurse with strong clinical footing will answer without hesitation.

What does a concierge nurse do that my doctors don’t?

A concierge nurse does not replace or compete with your existing care team. Most physicians operate in a traditional system that doesn’t allow for the kind of sustained, individualized attention most aging adults actually need. Let me explain:

A primary care physician may see a patient two to three times a year. A specialist sees them for a specific problem. No one in that system is responsible for the space in between. The medications that have quietly accumulated across multiple prescribers, the follow-up that didn't happen after a hospitalization, the slow functional changes that don't rise to the level of a complaint but signal something is changing.

That in-between space is where your concierge nurse works. The role is coordinative and preventive, not procedural. It's making sure the full picture is visible to someone with the clinical background to interpret it, so that families aren't left translating medical information on their own.

Why a retainer model? What if we don’t need continuous services?

This is more of a Counsel-specific question, not all concierge services are built on a retainer model of care. The reason that Counsel stresses service retainers is because we believe in continuity of care. The value of ongoing clinical oversight comes from knowing and developing a professional relationship with our clients over time. Understanding their baseline, patterns, providers, and family dynamics. That kind of knowledge doesn't transfer well from visit to visit if there's no consistent relationship underneath it.

That said, it's worth asking any concierge service how they handle situations where the level of need changes. At Counsel, service tiers are designed to scale. A client who needs light monthly oversight is structured differently than one navigating a complex post-hospitalization recovery. The retainer model shouldn't feel like a locked contract; it should feel like a relationship that adjusts as circumstances do.

If a family's situation is genuinely episodic like a specific transition or a short recovery period, it's worth having an honest conversation about whether ongoing services are the right fit at all. A concierge nurse who is straightforward about that is one worth trusting.

What does “clinical oversight” actually look like?

At Counsel, ongoing clinical oversight means regular in-home visits with nursing assessment, medication management, coordination with the client's existing providers, preparation for upcoming appointments, and consistent communication with family members who aren't always present. It means being reachable when a question comes up between visits, not as an emergency line, but as a clinical resource for the non-urgent concerns that otherwise go unaddressed or send families to wandering the internet late at night.

The standard for what you are receiving should be explicit before services begin. Ask for a description of what a typical month looks like, what communication you can expect, and what the nurse is actually assessing during visits. Vague answers to specific questions are worth noting.

What happens if something changes, and I need more or less support?

Aging isn't linear, and the level of clinical oversight a family needs in January may look very different by August.

Ask how the nurse or nursing service handles a significant health event like a hospitalization, a new diagnosis, or a fall. Ask what the process looks like for stepping up the level of service when circumstances become more complex, and equally, what happens if a client stabilizes and the family wants to scale back.

The answer should reflect a practice built around the client's actual needs rather than a fixed service package. Flexibility is what makes ongoing oversight sustainable for families over the long term.

These are the questions I'd want any family to bring to a conversation with Counsel or any concierge nurse they're considering. The right provider will welcome them.

To talk through your family’s situation, Request Private Consultation.

pages.title: Beyond Home Health: A Different Approach to Aging at Home
pages.description: Concierge nursing fills the gap that home health, caregiving, and primary care leave behind. Learn how ongoing clinical oversight supports aging adults at home

blocks.html:
Understanding the Landscape of Care

There are many options for supporting an aging parent at home and even more confusion about what each one actually does. It’s worth differentiating the landscape before talking about where concierge nursing fits within it.

Home health is a Medicare-funded, physician-ordered service designed to treat a specific, acute condition in the home setting. A patient qualifies when they are homebound and require skilled nursing or therapy to address a defined clinical need, such as wound care after surgery, physical therapy following a hip replacement, or IV antibiotics for an infection. It's skilled, important work, delivered within a tightly defined scope. But when the goal is met, the service ends.

Private caregiving fills a different need. Assistance with daily tasks like bathing, dressing, meal preparation, transportation, and companionship. Caregivers provide essential support for daily functioning, but they're not clinicians. They're not assessing medication interactions, interpreting lab results, or coordinating between a cardiologist and a primary care physician.

Primary care physicians are the cornerstone of any older adult's healthcare team, but the reality of modern medicine is that appointment windows are short, patient panels are large, and the space between visits is long. A good PCP is invaluable, but they can't be everywhere.

Each of these services was designed to do something specific. The challenge is that aging rarely stays within those boundaries.

The Gap Nobody Warned You About

Here’s a scenario I’ve seen countless times:

An older adult (let’s say a 78-year-old woman living alone) has a serious fall. She breaks her hip. There’s surgery, a hospital stay, a stint in a rehab facility, and then, finally, she gets to go home. Home health comes in several times a week for a month or so. She progresses. She meets her therapy goals. Home health discharges her.

On paper, she's recovered. In reality, she’s left with a complicated medication regimen she doesn't fully understand, follow-up appointments with multiple providers that nobody is helping her coordinate, and a bathroom that still doesn't have grab bars. Her daughter lives three states away, has taken two weeks off work already, and has three kids of her own. Her neighbors check in on her when they can.

The clinical support is gone, but the clinical complexity is not. And slowly things start to fall through the cracks.

This isn't a failure of any individual service. It's a huge gap in the overall system. Home health did what it was designed to do. The caregivers are doing what they were hired to do. The PCP is managing what they can in the time they have. But nobody is looking at the full picture and making sure it holds together.

These are the gaps that Counsel is designed to fill.

Concierge Nursing Is Different

It’s not episodic. It’s not tied to a diagnosis or a recovery goal. It’s not bound by the constraints of Medicare.

It’s an ongoing clinical relationship with a comprehensive understanding of the entire picture: medical history, medications, providers, appointments, home environment, family dynamics, routines, and goals. We stay in the picture, month after month, as an experienced set of eyes to help guide the way.

That means reviewing medications when something new is prescribed. Preparing or even joining a client for an upcoming appointment. Following up to make sure recommendations are acted on. Catching early signs before they become a hospitalization.

We know this individual by more than just their medical record.

It's proactive by design, because the goal isn't to respond to a crisis. The goal is to prevent one.

Who It’s Actually For

Our concierge model isn’t for everyone.

It's specifically designed for adults who are living independently at home, but whose medical complexity, medication regimen, or care coordination needs have outgrown what any single service or provider can manage. It's for families who are geographically distant, professionally busy, or simply overwhelmed by the volume of information they're expected to understand. It's for those who want a trusted clinical partner, not just another service provider.

It works alongside everything that is already in place: the primary care physician, the caregivers, the specialists. Someone who understands the full clinical landscape and helps your family navigate it with clarity and confidence.

Peace of Mind

Caring for an aging parent while managing your own career, your own family, your own life is genuinely hard. The medical system is complex and fragmented. Providers don't always talk to each other. Discharge instructions are written for clinicians, not families. Medications interact in ways that aren't obvious. Somewhere in the middle of all of it is your parent or loved one, trying to maintain their independence and dignity, while those who care most worry from a distance.

Concierge nursing doesn't solve everything. But it puts a clinical expert in your corner. Someone who really knows your loved one, understands the system, and is paying attention.

If you find yourself managing more than feels manageable, or simply wondering whether there's a better way to support someone you love, I'd encourage you to consider what ongoing clinical support could change.

pages.title: The Fall That Changes Everything — And How to Prevent it
pages.description: A registered nurse explains the most common fall hazards at home for aging parents and what families can do this week to reduce risk. Nashville, TN.

blocks.html:
No one plans for a fall. There’s no warning sign or alarm that goes off before it happens. One moment, your loved one is walking to the bathroom at two in the morning. Next, they’re on the floor, desperate for help.

Throughout my career, I’ve seen this exact story play out more times than I’d like to count. What strikes me every time is how preventable most falls are, not with expensive medical equipment or a complete home renovation, but with attention to small things that are so often overlooked.

Why Falls Matter More Than Most Families Realize

Falls are the leading cause of injury-related hospitalization in adults over the age of 65. The real impact goes far beyond the hospitalization itself.

Example: A hip fracture leads to surgery, which leads to weeks of rehabilitation, which ultimately leads to a level of dependence that did not exist before the fall.

Many older adults never fully return to their prior level of independence after a serious fall. The trajectory shifts. Sometimes permanently.

And then there’s fear. After a fall, many older adults become afraid of falling again. They move less. They avoid activities they used to enjoy. They become more isolated. That fear alone can accelerate decline faster than the injury itself.

For families, a fall is often the event that forces a conversation no one was ready to have. Conversations about safety, independence, and what might come next. It doesn’t have to be this way. Let’s talk about a solution.

What We Look for When We Walk Into a Home

One of the first things we assess when visiting a client isn’t their medication list or their blood pressure. It’s their environment. The home itself tells a story about risk, and most families are surprised by how many hazards are hiding in plain sight.

The floors. Throw rugs are one of the most common fall hazards we encounter. They slide, bunch up, catch the edge of a shoe or a walker, etc. Hardwood floors with loose rugs, bathroom mats without non-slip backing, and unsecured runners in hallways are fall hazards. Luckily, the fix is super simple: remove them or secure them with non-slip pads or double-sided tape.

The lighting. Many falls happen at night, on the way to the bathroom or the kitchen. If the path from the bedroom to the bathroom is dark, the risk of a fall increases significantly. Nightlights plugged into outlets along that route, motion-activated lights in hallways, and a lamp within easy reach of the bed can make an enormous difference. Adequate lighting is one of the cheapest and most effective fall prevention measures there is.

The bathroom. Wet surfaces, awkward transitions in and out of the tub or shower, and no grab bars to hold onto all increase the risk of a fall. We look for grab bars installed near the toilet and inside the shower, non-slip floor surfaces, and the method of entrance into the shower or tub. If your loved one is using a towel bar for balance or support, that is a red flag. Towel bars are not designed to support body weight and can pull right out of the wall. The installation of grab bars and non-slip floor mats is a great start to minimizing fall risk in the bathroom.

The stairs. Stairs are manageable for most older adults when the environment supports safe navigation. Are handrails present on both sides? Are they sturdy? Is anything stored on the stairs (shoes, books, laundry) that creates an obstacle? Are the edges of the steps clearly visible, or do they blend together in low light?

Footwear. Yes, footwear in the house. This one often surprises people. What your loved one wears on their feet inside the home matters. Socks on hardwood floors are slippery and are just as much of a risk as a wet bathroom floor. Worn-out slippers that have no traction and shoes that are too loose can catch on carpet and rugs. Proper-fitting, non-slip footwear is a simple change that meaningfully reduces risk.

The Medication Factor

Not all fall risks are environmental. Some are pharmaceutical.

Many common medications prescribed to older adults can cause dizziness, lightheadedness, or drops in blood pressure, especially when standing up. Blood pressure medications, sedatives, sleep aids, antidepressants, and even antihistamines can all increase fall risk. When someone is on multiple medications, these side effects can compound.

We review our clients’ full medication list with fall risk in mind and recommend that families not utilizing our services do the same with a physician and/or pharmacist. It’s a conversation that doesn’t happen as often as it should, and sometimes a simple adjustment, such as changing the timing of a dose or switching to an alternative medication, can significantly reduce risk.

If your parent or loved one has started a new medication recently and seems unsteady or mentions feeling dizzy, don’t brush it off. Bring it up with their provider.

What Families Can Do Right Now

You don’t need a professional assessment to get started, though one can certainly help. Here’s what I’d encourage any family to do in the next few days:

Walk through your parent’s home with fresh eyes. Don’t walk through as their child who’s been there hundreds of times. Walk through as if you’re seeing it for the first time, looking specifically for anything that could cause a trip, slip, or loss of balance.

Check the path from the bedroom to the bathroom at night. Turn off the lights and walk it yourself. If you can’t see clearly, neither can they.

Look at the bathroom. Are there grab bars? Non-slip surfaces? A way to get in and out of the shower safely?

Look down at the floors. Loose rugs, clutter, cords running across walkways. Remove or secure anything that could catch a foot.

Ask about their shoes. What are they wearing around the house? If it’s socks or worn-out slippers, it might be time for a change.

Ask about dizziness. Have they been lightheaded recently? Unsteady? Have they had any near-misses they haven’t mentioned? Most older adults will not volunteer this information because of the worry it might bring to their family or the fear of losing independence in their home.

Prevention Is Quiet Work

Fall prevention is one of the most valuable things a family can invest in for an aging parent. It preserves independence, it avoids crisis, and gives everyone involved something that’s hard to put a price on: peace of mind.

blocks.html:
Our Practice

Counsel Concierge Nursing is a Nashville, Tennessee-based concierge nursing practice providing private nursing oversight for adults and their families. Our services focus on personalized clinical oversight, care coordination, and advocacy. Our mission is to preserve independence and autonomy while offering families clarity and confidence outside the constraints of traditional healthcare settings and service models.

We serve Nashville and the surrounding Middle Tennessee area, offering private, concierge nursing services tailored to each client’s unique circumstances. Our nursing philosophy is shaped by years of clinical experience and a belief that wellness and independence deserve thoughtful, individualized support.
Our Story

My name is Gus, and I am the founder of Counsel Concierge Nursing.

I have spent the majority of my nursing career in critical care, emergency, and surgical settings, caring for patients with complex and evolving medical needs.

After years of bedside nursing across multiple specialties and healthcare systems, I kept noticing the same challenge: families navigating complex health conditions between multiple providers, managing medication changes after every appointment, and feeling completely lost in a fragmented system that wasn’t designed for coordination.

I founded Counsel to bridge the gap.

Our standard is a comprehensive understanding of each client’s entire clinical picture from complex diagnoses to simple wellness habits.

From continuous nursing oversight to situational services, our goal is to help clients and families navigate healthcare with confidence and peace of mind.
Augustus Osgood, BSN, RN
Founder, Counsel Concierge Nursing

blocks.html: Private Consultation

The private consultation is the foundation of the Counsel care model. This consultation allows us to understand the individual’s health history, functionality, independence, and overall goals, while providing families with clarity on whether our services are the right fit for their needs.

This is not a sales meeting. It is a professional clinical assessment and coordinating discussion designed to ensure thoughtful, appropriate engagement.

Initial Introduction

All services begin with a complimentary discovery call to determine appropriateness. When helpful, a brief introductory meeting may be arranged to ensure mutual alignment prior to proceeding with a comprehensive consultation.

If Counsel is a suitable fit, a private in-person consultation is scheduled.

What to Expect During Consultation

The consultation is a comprehensive, collaborative session with the patient and family that includes:

  • Review of health history and current/future concerns

  • Assessment of functional independence and support needs

  • Discussion of goals, preferences, priorities

  • Identification of potential risks and opportunities for proactive planning

  • Overview of how concierge services may be structured

Following the consultation, we will create a personalized care plan outlining recommended nursing scope, level of involvement, and next steps.

Consultation Request

Please complete this form to request a private consultation. This initial inquiry helps us understand your needs and determine how we may best support you. All inquiries are handled with discretion, and we will follow up directly.

Private consultations are available in Nashville and surrounding areas.

blocks.html: Services

Counsel Concierge Nursing offers private, professional nursing oversight for independent adults who prioritize consistency and proactive care. We support aging in place while providing families with assurances of clinical expertise and professionalism.

We operate on a private-pay model, allowing care to be tailored to each client’s unique circumstances without the constraints of traditional home health or insurance-based services.

Situational clinical support outside of standard service arrangements is offered on an individual basis following consultation.
Monthly Retainer Services

Following an initial consultation, a retainer is structured around the specific oversight, coordination, and clinical support your situation requires. Listed below is the full scope of services available.

items.title: Care Coordination
items.html: Provider communication & follow-through. Direct communication with primary care and specialist teams to ensure recommendations are understood, followed, and coordinated across providers.

items.title: Care Transitions
items.html: Discharge & recovery support. Structured oversight during the high-risk post-discharge & post-surgical window. Medication review, follow-up coordination, and early identification of complications.

items.title: Medication Management
items.html: Comprehensive reconciliation of all medication, including OTC and supplements, with attention to interactions, high-risk agents, and compliance.

items.title: Chronic Disease Management
items.html: Clinical monitoring and management of chronic disease. Living with chronic conditions requires consistent, knowledgeable oversight. Whether you're managing a single condition or navigating the complexity of several at once, we provide the clinical expertise and personal attention that helps you stay ahead of your health.

items.title: Appointment Accompaniment
items.html: Appointment preparation, accompaniment, and follow-up. Pre-visit preparation to maximize clinical encounters, in-person accompaniment as appropriate, and post-visit follow-up with the family.

items.title: Caregiving & Companionship
items.html: ADL assistance and company. While providing professional, supportive nursing services, we assist with ADLs and provide several opportunities for companionship (walks, errands, meals).

items.title: Education
items.html: Thorough teaching and instruction gives our clients the tools and comprehension they need to become active participants in their care.

blocks.html:
Situational Clinical Support

In certain circumstances, we provide case-specific, clinical involvement outside of standard service arrangements. Availability and pricing are determined on an individual basis following consultation. When appropriate, this may include:

Travel

We help clients and families prepare for travel with the same attention we'd bring to any care transition.

  • Packing medication and preparing any needed medical supplies

  • Notifying care team

  • Anticipating needs before departure

  • Accompanying clients and families on business or leisure travel

Hospital & Home Health Transitions

We support clients and families through the hospital stay and the days that follow.

  • Communicating with the care team

  • Participating in rounds with family

  • Overnight presence and support when needed

Afterwards, we support a safe discharge:

  • medication reconciliation

  • follow-up appointments

  • monitoring for early signs of setback

Pre & Post-Surgical Support

Post-operative recovery in the comfort of your home. We prepare clients and families in the days before surgery.

  • Understanding & setting expectations

  • Preparing the home for a safe and comfortable recovery

  • Compliance with pre-procedure orders

Post-op, we provide in-home monitoring, support, and coordination through recovery

  • Monitoring for complications

  • Medication reconciliation

  • Communication with surgical team
What Our Services Are — and Are Not

• Private, concierge nursing services & oversight

  • Proactive, relationship-based support

  • Designed to preserve independence and aging in place for clients and families
Counsel is:

• A home health or skilled nursing agency

  • Task-based personal care

  • Insurance based care
Counsel is not:

Not Sure Where to Start?

That’s exactly what your consultation is for. All services begin with a complimentary discovery call to assess suitability and appropriateness of our services, followed by a private in-person consultation to evaluate needs and create a personalized care plan.

Frequently Asked Questions

Have additional questions? Request Private Consultation.

items.title: Is Counsel covered by Medicare or private insurance?
items.html: No. Counsel operates entirely on a private-pay basis. It allows our services to be proactive, flexible, and structured around the client's actual needs rather than coverage criteria.

items.title: How is Counsel different from home health or a home care agency?
items.html: Home health provides skilled nursing services ordered by a physician and billed through insurance. Home care agencies provide non-clinical caregiving: bathing, meals, companionship. Counsel operates differently. Services are private-pay, ongoing, and clinical in nature, focused on oversight, coordination, and proactive management rather than task completion or episodic skilled care.

items.title: How is this different from a geriatric care manager?
items.html: Geriatric care managers are typically social workers or nurses who assess needs and arrange services. Counsel provides direct, ongoing clinical nursing oversight — not a one-time assessment or a referral to other services. The relationship is continuous and clinically active.

items.title: How do we know if Counsel is the right fit?
items.html: Most Counsel clients are independent adults managing one or more chronic conditions, often with adult children or family members who are geographically distant or professionally occupied. Families typically come to Counsel after a hospitalization, a concerning diagnosis, or the recognition that navigating the healthcare system on their own is no longer sustainable. We work best with proactive families who value time and peace of mind.

items.title: What does the initial consultation process look like?
items.html: Every consultation request begins with a complimentary discovery call to assess appropriateness. The initial consultation is a focused clinical assessment and family meeting conducted in the home to assess the client's current health status, health history, medications, functional independence, and family goals. It concludes with a written care plan and recommended retainer structure. There is no obligation to proceed with our services at the conclusion of the consultation process.

items.title: Can the level of service change over time?
items.html: Yes. Client needs evolve. Our retainer structure is designed to flex in either direction based on what the clinical situation requires.

blocks.html:
Privacy Policy

Effective Date: December 16, 2025

Counsel Concierge Nursing, LLC ("Counsel," "we," "our," or "us") respects your privacy and is committed to protecting the personal information you provide when visiting our website or contacting us.

This Privacy Policy describes how we collect, use, store, and protect information obtained through our website and inquiry forms.

1. Scope of This Policy

This website is intended for informational purposes only. Counsel Concierge Nursing does not provide medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment through this website.

Submission of information through this website does not establish a nurse–patient relationship or any clinical care relationship.

Counsel Concierge Nursing operates as a private-pay concierge nursing oversight service and is not an insurance-based home health agency.

2. Information We Collect

We may collect limited personal information that you voluntarily provide, including:

pages.title: Post-Operative Recovery Care
pages.description: In-home post-op nursing care in Nashville — pre-op preparation, post-operative monitoring and coordination.

blocks.html: Post-Operative Recovery Care

Surgery ends in the operating room. Recovery happens at home. That transition is often where the most avoidable complications occur. Counsel provides private, in-home nursing support before the procedure, immediately after discharge, and through the days that follow.

We work directly with your surgical team to ensure nothing is missed between the operating room and a full recovery.
Before Surgery

We prepare clients and families in the days leading up to a procedure, so the recovery period starts on a solid clinical foundation.

  • Reviewing pre-procedure orders and ensuring compliance

  • Preparing the home for a safe, comfortable recovery

  • Setting expectations for what the first days home will look like

  • Coordinating with family or caregivers on their role during recovery
After Surgery

Once discharged, we provide structured, in-home clinical oversight through the recovery window.

  • In-home monitoring for the earliest signs of complication

  • Medication reconciliation and management

  • Wound and incision observation

  • Direct line of communication with your surgical team

  • Coordination of follow-up appointments

  • Support and education for family caregivers
Who This Is For

Post-operative recovery support with Counsel is appropriate for clients recovering from a range of surgical procedures. Particularly when:

  • The client lives alone or without a caregiver present around the clock

  • Family is out of town or unable to provide clinical-level oversight

  • The procedure carries a higher risk of post-operative complication

  • The family wants a clinical set of eyes during recovery to provide peace of mind
Investment

Day-of-surgery RN accompaniment, from pickup to recovery at home, starts at $750. For clients who need continued support beyond the day of surgery, we offer extended recovery packages, including overnight and multi-day continuous care, structured around the procedure, surgeon’s discharge instructions, and the client's specific recovery needs.

Every engagement begins with a consultation to confirm scope and pricing before care begins.

Frequently Asked Questions

Have additional questions? Request Private Consultation.

items.title: How soon after surgery can a nurse be involved?
items.html: We can begin as early as the pre-operative period, and our involvement typically starts the day of discharge. Engagements are scheduled around the surgery date, so we recommend reaching out as soon as a procedure is confirmed.

items.title: Is this covered by insurance?
items.html: No. Counsel operates on a private-pay basis, which allows care to be structured around the client's actual needs rather than insurance criteria. Post-operative support starts at $750 for day-of-surgery accompaniment, with extended and overnight care also available. Some clients use HSA/FSA funds; we recommend confirming eligibility with your plan administrator.

items.title: How is this different from home health after surgery?
items.html: Home health is ordered by a physician, billed through insurance, and limited to specific skilled visits. Counsel's post-operative support is private, flexible in scope and duration, and centered on continuous clinical oversight rather than episodic visits.

items.title: Will you communicate with my surgeon?
items.html: Yes, with the client's consent. We coordinate directly with the surgical team to ensure the recovery plan is being followed and to flag any concerns early.

items.title: How long does post-operative support typically last?
items.html: It depends on the procedure and the client's recovery. Some engagements last a few days; others extend several weeks. This is defined during the consultation and can be adjusted as recovery progresses.
